name: install
description: Set up a local MemQL cluster on this machine: check what it needs, install the supporting tools, make it reachable over https, start it, and finish with a way to sign in.

steps.description: Taking stock of this machine before anything is installed: what system it is, which supporting tools are already here, whether Docker is answering, whether the ports a cluster needs are free, and how much disk is left. Only a system MemQL cannot support stops the install here; the rest is reported for you to read.
Checking that Docker can run containers for you, before anything is installed.
Installing k3d, which runs the cluster, and checking the download is the expected one.
Installing kubectl, which talks to the cluster, and checking the download is the expected one.
Installing mkcert, which issues this machine's local certificates, and checking the download is the expected one.
Pointing the cluster's web addresses at this machine, inside a marked section of the system hosts file.
Setting up the tools your browsers need to trust this machine's local certificates.
steps.retainedReason: certutil is a general system tool other software uses. MemQL installs it because without it Firefox and Chrome cannot trust the local CA and the front door is unreachable in a browser -- but an application uninstaller that removes distribution packages is how installers earn their reputation, so this one is never taken back.

steps.description: Issuing the certificate that lets this cluster answer over https.
Downloading the MemQL release you chose.

Checking that your AI provider key is accepted, before the cluster is built around it. Skipped when you supplied none: installing spends no AI credit, and providers are set up afterwards in the portal.
Creating the cluster and starting MemQL's services in it.
Creating your owner account and applying the settings you gave, then restarting the services that read them.
Checking the cluster answers over https at every one of its addresses.
Looking for a sign-in link for the owner account, as a second way in. A cluster that has not been asked for one carries none, which is reported rather than treated as a failure.

Creating a single-use link for setting up a passkey on the owner account. This install names that owner as the cluster starts, so the link is normally ready here; a cluster started without owner details has nobody to enrol yet, and that is reported instead.

Claiming this cluster's recovery key and showing it once, so you finish with a way back in if every other is ever lost. The key is minted for the owner as the cluster starts, so a first install normally ends holding one; a cluster started without owner details has nobody to mint one for, and a key an earlier run already claimed is left alone, because only its fingerprint was kept and re-showing it is impossible.
